content.summary_of_the_paper: The co-existence of heterogeneous label noise and class-imbalance distribution in FL makes conventional label-noise learning methods ineffective. To address this problem, this paper proposes FEDCNI, which includes a noise-resilience local solver and a robust global aggregator. The local solver owns a prototypical classifier to detect the noisy samples. The global aggregator re-weights the aggregation from data-size to noise level in different learning period. Real-world datasets are used to verify the FEDCNI.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
1. Due to the heterogeneous environment of FL, the problem that this paper aims to solve exist in the real-world FL and is important.
2. The illustration of failures of small-loss noise detection on small and class-imbalanced local datasets is easy to understand and well illustrates that conventional methods cannot work in label-noise FL.
3. The experiment results show good test accuracy of FEDCNI.


Weaknesses
1. The proposed methods are combined from multiple different techniques. However, some techniques (i.e. Local Noise Detection, Curriculum Pseudo Labeling and Denoise Mixup Training) are simply borrowed from other areas, is there any challenge of using them into FL?
2. Some proposed techniques lack experimental or theoretical supports, e.g. "In FL, we found the learning periods are also important, therefore, we elaborate different losses for the local solvers in the early and late period.".  Is there any evidence to that show learning periods are important in FL? And for the Section 4.3, how do you verify that the early phase of FEDAVG does NOT need to cautiously learn from noisy samples and clients?
3. Except 1 and 2, Prototype Generation is the technique that is the mostly relevant to FL, which is proposed by other works. And authors propose local prototype generation, which is used in centralized noisy-label learning methods. Overall, the FEDCNI looks like a simple combination of multiple methods, which decreases the novelty of this paper.
4. The proposed methods aim to improve the generalization performance, but lack theoretical analysis on generalization performance.

content.title: Response to Reviewer WMvh (2/2):
content.comment:
- **Q3: The novelty of this paper.**
- **A3:** Thank you for your constructive comments.  We are sorry to cause the misunderstanding that the reviewers may think of our work as a simple combination of multiple methods. Here, we would like to give full clarification about our novelty.
    - **The problem difficulty of noisy-label FL.** Unlike centralized noisy-label learning, FL with noisy labels is a complex and challenging problem, and it at least has the following unique challenges. **(1) Complex data environment.** As we stated in the paper, clients in FL have different data sizes, different noise levels, and different class imbalance degrees (Non-IID data).  **(2) Complex system environment.** Instead of distributed SGD, the clients in FL conduct local training with multiple local epochs, which raises the difficulty in convergence. The server aggregates the local models into a global one, but clients have different data quantity and quality and even local epochs, which makes the aggregation complicated. Therefore, tackling FL with noisy labels requires a systematic algorithms design rather than a single technique, and we remind that the methods in previous works all consist of multiple modules [3-5]. In this paper, we give a systematic solution in which we **critically learn from local noisy samples** (*noise detection, pseudo labeling, and robust local loss*) and **critically learn from global clients** (*the robust aggregator in different learning periods*). Although there are multiple modules in the solution, they are naturally motivated and closely related rather than a simple combination.
    - **Significant empirical improvement.** The systematic solution we proposed has shown significant empirical improvement **over all baselines**. Moreover, it even has close results to **FedAvg without noisy labels** (see Figure 2 (a) and (b)), which may be the theoretical accuracy upper bound of FL noisy-label learning. The effectiveness of our method and the significant improvement is also recognized by reviewers ojgr and Lk77. 
    - **Providing insights to the community.** Apart from the experimental improvement, our novelty also roots in the enriched insights. Firstly, for noise detection, we show that the ***local prototypical*** method is effective enough in FL with noisy labels. Previous works resort to the small-loss trick, and it fails in the small, imbalanced, and noisy local datasets of clients. Other works adopting prototypical methods all use *global prototype sharing*, but it may cause privacy concerns. In this work, we find the local prototype is effective enough, and it is also robust. Secondly, we bring insights into ***Mixup*** that treating noisy and clean samples differently can improve performance, and we also find that using Mixup appropriately can reduce the need for vanilla CE loss. Thirdly, we introduce the concept of ***different learning periods in noisy-label FL*** and provide a simple aggregation method by switching the aggregation schemes in the early and late. Such a simple try is insightful, and it can inspire more future works to explore the training dynamics in the learning periods of noisy-label FL. We hope these insights are valuable to the community and are solid enough to show our novelty.
- **Q4: Lack of theoretical analysis.**
- **A4:** Thanks for the suggestion. Our paper is mainly an empirical work in which we propose an effective algorithm tackling FL noisy-label issues and show its experimental superiority. The theoretical analysis is not our contribution. It is also worth noting that due to the complexity of the FL noisy-label learning system, there is currently no work with theoretical analysis, and we reckon the theory may deserve a separate paper.

### Reference

[1] Han B, Yao Q, Yu X, et al. Co-teaching: Robust training of deep neural networks with extremely noisy labels. *In Proceedings of* Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems ((NeurIPS), 2018.

[2] Li J, Socher R, Hoi S C H. DivideMix: Learning with Noisy Labels as Semi-supervised Learning. *In Proceedings of* International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). 2019.

[3] Xu J, Chen Z, Quek T Q S, et al. FedCorr: Multi-Stage Federated Learning for Label Noise Correction. *In Proceedings of* the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). 2022.

[4] Yang S, Park H, Byun J, et al. Robust federated learning with noisy labels. IEEE Intelligent Systems, 2022, 37(2): 35-43.

[5] Fang X, Ye M. Robust Federated Learning With Noisy and Heterogeneous Clients. *In Proceedings of* the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). 2022.

[6] Shen Y, Sanghavi S. Learning with bad training data via iterative trimmed loss minimization. *In Proceedings of* International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML). PMLR, 2019.

[7] Yan G, Wang H, Li J. Critical Learning Periods in Federated Learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2109.05613, 2021.

content.title: Response to Reviewer WMvh (1/2):
content.comment:
We are glad to hear from the reviewer that our topic is important, our method is described clearly, and the results show good performance. We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comments and provide detailed response as follows.

- **Q1: The sentence "_Some techniques (i.e. Local Noise Detection, Curriculum Pseudo Labeling and Denoise Mixup Training) are simply borrowed from other areas, is there any challenge of using them into FL?_"**
- **A1:** Thank you for this insightful comment. We want to first clarify that the methods are not  simply borrowed from other areas. The modules in our method are structured from relevant noisy label learning works with consideration of unique challenges in FL scenarios. Then, we present the challenges in FL.
    - **Local Noise Detection:** In centralized noisy learning, the dataset is large enough to apply some tricks. While in FL, local data is small and class-imbalanced, which prevents the simply borrowing noise detection such as small-loss. As we shown in Table 1, simply deploying the centralized noisy-label learning methods (Co-teaching [1] and DivideMix [2]) in FL will have bad performances. In our study, we devise the local prototypical method which is novel and effective in FL's scenarios.
    - **Dynamic Thresholds (Curriculum Pseudo Labeling):** The module of dynamic thresholds is naturally designed to tackle the FL’s unique challenge that every client has different class-wise quantity, noise level, and learning difficulty. If we set a unified threshold for all classes in all clients, it will result in bad pseudo-labeling and bad convergence. Although the dynamic threshold method is inspired by curriculum pseudo labeling in semi-supervised learning, we have a more adaptive use in FL, since the primary work only concerns the natural learning difficulty of each class in centralized learning.
    - **Denoise Mixup Training:** Mixup is indeed a general trick to improve performance in noisy label learning as we mention in the paper. However, we improve vanilla mixup to better adopt the FL’s settings. In federated noisy learning, we should carefully treat local small data size and make full use of the above noise detection. In a contrastive view, we mix a noise sample with a clean one which belongs to the pseudo label class of the noisy one, and it reduces the effects of wrong labels.
    
- The effectiveness of all the above mentioned modules can be proved in Table 4 about the ablation study. 
    
- **Q2: Evidence of critical learning periods in FL. & Whether the early phase of FL needs to cautiously learn from noisy samples and clients.**
- **A2:** Thanks for the comment. We apologize for the confusion of critical learning periods that may occur in Section 4, and we have reorganized Section 4 for better presentation. In the revision, there are two places where we consider a switching round. The first is at the end of Section 4.1, where we consider a switching round $T_{s_1}$. Before $T_{s_1}$, the accuracy of pseudo labeling is relatively low, so we use to assign the pseudo labels to the noisy samples just after $T_{s_1}$. The second is at the beginning of Section 4.3, where we consider another switching round $T_{s_2}$ for aggregating differently in different learning periods. We also mentioned in the revised version that for simplicity reasons, we set $T_{s}=T_{s_1}=T_{s_2}$, so there is only one hyper-parameter of switching round. We have added pieces of evidence to support why $T_{s_1}$ is needed (Figure 9 of the appendix) and how performance improves when $T_{s_2}$ exists (Table 7 and Figure 10 of the appendix). It is also worth mentioning that $T_s$ is relatively small compared with the whole training round $T$ (e.g. $T_s=15, ~T=100$), which indicates that we assume a short early learning period.
- About the critical learning periods, as we stated in the first paragraph of Section 4.3 (current version), the learning periods in noisy-label learning have theoretical guarantees [6]. Also, the learning periods in FL are also evidential [7] (we have included this citation as a footnote on page 6 of the new version). But the learning periods in FL with noisy labels are not discovered in previous works. In this paper, we have made a simple try to apply different aggregation strategies in the early and late and found they can empirically prove performance. We reckon this discovery is insightful and novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Federated learning faces many challenges including class imbalance and label noise. The authors propose an algorithm named FedCNI to tackle these problems. It includes a local solver, and a global aggregator. The local solver detects noisy data ... and estimates the noise level of clients, which the global aggregator reweights the client models based on their noise level and data size. The algorithm is empirically evaluated on multiple datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 

- The paper is easy to follow. 
- The challenge is clear and the motivation is straight-forward. 
- Empirical illustration verifies that local solver of FedCNI can detect noisy label better than small-loss with local model. 
- Empirical evaluation under multiple dataset / class imbalance level / noise level verify the effectiveness of FedCNI. 

Weaknesses: 

- The authors claim that the under class imbalance the local model has higher confidence on majority class, which bias the noisy label detection. However, it seems like using the global model, which is trained on the union of all clients' data, is an easy solution of this. 
- Reliability under highly skewed label distribution: I am curious why FedCNI can deal with label imbalance better than the baselines (especially the one I proposed before). Consider that a client has two labels of data, 90% positive and 10% negative. When the noise level is 10%, there will be 81% with positive GT and positive label, 9% with positive GT and negative label, 9% with negative GT and negative label, 1% with negative GT and positive label. Then among all data with negative label, half of them are actually positive while half of then are negative. It seems like under this setting, even the prototype $$p_{k, c}$$ cannot be computed robustly.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is well-written and easy to follow. 

Quality: FedCNI has clear motivation, reasonable algorithm design and plausible effectiveness. While I have several questions about why FedCNI is more effective than baselines. 

Novelty: The proposed method is a novel work tackling class imbalance and label noise simulaneously. However the novelty may be overclaimed since baseline algorithms like Fedcorr also test their algorithms under class imbalance data partition. 

Reproducibility: Although code is not released, the author explain their algorithm in detail with pseudo-code.
content.summary_of_the_review: It is an effective algorithm tackling a new setting under class imbalance and noisy label challenges. It would be good if the authors could provide intuition on why the local solver is more robust to noises.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Lk77:
content.comment:
We are delighted to receive the positive feedback that our paper is well-written and our method has clear motivation, reasonable algorithm design and plausible effectiveness. We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comments and provide detailed response as follows.

- **Q1: The sentences "_The authors claim that the under class imbalance the local model has higher confidence on majority class, which bias the noisy label detection. However, it seems like using the global model, which is trained on the union of all clients' data, is an easy solution of this._"**
- **A1:** Thanks for the comments. Our noise detection is conducted in every client’s local epoch, and in the beginning epoch of local training, the initially received global model is used. As the local training is conducted, the local model will be more biased on the imbalanced dataset, but dynamic noise detection in each epoch is also needed, where we find the small-loss trick fails. Therefore, our prototypical method is also necessary.
- **Q2: Reliability under highly skewed label distribution.**
- **A2:** Thanks for the reviewer’s insightful comment. We understand the reviewer’s concern, you may probably mean that if the noise level is high in minority class, how can the local prototypical noise detection be effective, especially in the raised scenario where the samples denoted as the minority class are half clean and half noisy. Firstly, the initial global model in the start of local training will enable the clients to have a better representation on the minority class. Secondly, if the representation is satisfactory, the clean samples will have similar embeddings and strengthen the embeddings with each other. While the noisy samples are from other classes and they are less directional and viewed as random vectors, so the average of these embeddings has smaller norm. Even in the extreme noise level (50%) as the reviewer mentioned, if the representation is effective, the clean averaged embedding will also dominate in mean prototype. Knowing that the embeddings are high-dimensional (512 in our paper) and resorting to the fact that any two high-dimensional random vectors are most probably orthogonal, the cosine similarities between the noisy embeddings and the mean prototype are likely to be closer to zero, while the clean samples will have higher cosine values, closer to 1. Hence, the cosine similarities of the clean and noisy are distinguishable. We have provided more evidential results about the noise detection precision and recall of each client in Figures 6-8 in appendix. It is obvious that for the clients with large noise ratios, the precision of noise detection is high and the recall is relatively low, and the overall noise detection is satisfactory.
- **Q3: The sentence "_However the novelty may be overclaimed since baseline algorithms like Fedcorr also test their algorithms under class imbalance data partition._"**
- **A3:** Thanks for the comment. We apologize for the unclear delivery which may cause the reviewer’s misunderstanding. We have rewritten the relevant sentences in the introduction and related works. Actually, we are trying to say that we have studied further into the class imbalance (Non-IID) issue in FL noisy-label learning. We give following evidence to support our novelty.
    - We want to point out that FedCorr’s [1] experiments are mainly conducted in IID settings with only one small table of Non-IID CIFAR-10; RoFL [2] and RHFL [3] both adopt IID settings. We conduct all experiments under Non-IID data distribution.
    - In the view of methods, FedCorr [1] does not take class imbalance into prudent consideration in noise detection. The bad performance of small-loss method has also been demonstrated in Figure 1 and Section 5.3-Noise Detection performance. Our method truly considers the class imbalance: crafting an robust noise detection for skewed data, and dynamic thresholds which consider class-wise data size, noise level and learning difficulty.
    - We do not want to overclaim novelty in class imbalance. But, we indeed deal with FL noise label problem with facing and considering of Non-IIDness (local class imbalance) by giving targeted approaches and massive experiments, instead of avoiding this critical phenomenon in FL.

### Reference

[1] Xu J, Chen Z, Quek T Q S, et al. FedCorr: Multi-Stage Federated Learning for Label Noise Correction. *In Proceedings of* the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). 2022: 10184-10193.

[2] Yang S, Park H, Byun J, et al. Robust federated learning with noisy labels. IEEE Intelligent Systems, 2022, 37(2): 35-43.

[3] Fang X, Ye M. Robust Federated Learning With Noisy and Heterogeneous Clients. *In Proceedings of* the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). 2022: 10072-10081.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies federated learning with noisy label problems. Specifically, for each client, the proposed method uses the similarity between the individual embedding and the mean of the embedding as the indicator of whether the data is likely to be a noisy sample. Then, a two-component GMM is used to detect those samples. Also, the dynamic threshold is used to modify the label of those predicted noisy samples.
In the late stage of FL, the author recalibrates the aggregation process to alleviate the effect of noisy samples.  Experiments show the proposed method is more effective than some baselines in certain scenarios.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

The idea is easy to follow
The experiment result shows the proposed method can defend against flipping and uniform label noise.

Weakness:

The method seems to be ad-hoc. I doubt whether this method can be applied in a more general way. Below are my questions about the method:

 Equation 6 defines the mean embeddings, and it will be used to calculate the similarity later. The underlying assumption here is that this mean represents the clean representation. My question is, how do the authors guarantee this embedding result is trustable given the existence of the noisy label samples?  What if the noisy representation is single-clustered? What if the noisy representation is very far away from the true mean? Both cases can make the mean embedding very bad. In your experiment, the uniform flipping and pair-wise flipping cannot generate single-clustered embedding, and I doubt that is the reason why your method works well. I wish the author could clarify this assumption or provide more motivation for why using simple empirical means of representation works in a more principled way.

two-component GMM: The usage of two-component GMM also assumes the noisy sample embedding and clean sample embeddings are two gaussian, which is unrealistic. It is worth investigating other non-parametric methods here

The dynamic thresholding is based on the previous similarity results, So I have the same concern here. Can this method easily generalize to other types of noisy-label situations?

For the experiment part, my main question is as follows:
Does each client use the same strategy for the pairwise flip? This is very important, and it would be great if the author could provide the results for both cases (i.e. use the same or different pairwise flipping strategy across the client).

content.comment:
- **Q3: Other types of noisy-label situations.**
- **A3:** Thank you for the valuable comment. We would like to clarify that our noisy-label settings are thorough compared with previous works, especially FL with noisy label. We list the noisy-label settings of both centralized and federated learning in previous works as follows.

    | Method | Symmetric  | Pair | Naturally noised | Other  |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | PAL [1] | √ | √ |  |  |
    | RRL [2] | √ | √ |  | Out-of-distribution (OOD) images |
    | SMP [3] |  |  | √ |  |
    | APL [4] | √ | √ |  |  |
    | Co-teaching [5] | √ | √ |  |  |
    | DivideMix [6] | √ | √ | √ |  |
    | RoFL [7] | √ | √ |  |  |
    | FedCorr [8] | √ |  | √ |  |
    | RHFL [9] | √ | √ |  |  |
    | Ours | √ | √ | √ |  |

    *Note: Natural noise means datasets which is originally noisy, e.g. Clothing1M, WebVIsion and Food101-N. Utilizing out-of-distribution (OOD) images is a setting of mixture of different datasets, called the open set problem.*

    - It is found that symmetric flipping, pair (asymmetric)flipping noise and naturally noisy datasets are the most commonly used in label-noise research, and we adopted them all. There are also other types of unusual noise as heteroskedastic noise and instance dependent noise. We reckon our current settings might be sufficient to support the solidity, we would rather leave other noisy settings in future work.
- **Q4: Experiments about the same or different pairwise flipping strategy across the client.**
- **A4:** We find this comment very constructive. In our previous implementation, we followed the clients’ pairwise flipping in RoFL [5] and it adopts the same strategy across the clients. Each class are only changed to a fixed similar class (e.g. dog→cat, deer→horse). It equals a fixed mapping  like class 0 to class 9, class 1 to class 0, class 2 to class 1… The strategy is also the same for all clients.  As far as we know, no existing works have focused on what happens if clients adopt different mapping rules. We immediately conduct supplementary experiments in Section 5 Table 2. We presents the comparison with the same strategy as:

    | Method | Uniform strategy | Different strategy  |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | FedAvg | 80.58 | 84.40 |
    | FedProx | 79.63 | 84.95 |
    | FedDyn | 70.11 | 72.27 |
    | SCAFFOLD | 80.29 | 84.87 |
    | FedCorr | 76.24 | 77.16 |
    | RoFL | 81.37 | 85.32 |
    | FedProto | 80.09 | 86.45 |
    | FedAvg+DivideMix | 74.15 | 83.63 |
    | Ours | 86.13 | 88.85 |

    The results shows different strategies increase all methods’ performance. We infer that the former fixed pairwise flip makes a global misunderstanding which reduces the upper bound of expected accuracy. It is notable that our method still reaches SOTA in the setting where clients have different flipping strategies.

- **Q5: The experiment setting is not clear.**
- **A5:** Thanks for your reminder. In the revision, we have refined the Section 5.1-Implementation details. More details about settings and hyper-parameters have also been added in the Appendix A.1.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ojgr (1/2):
content.comment:
We appreciate that the reviewer finds our paper is easy to follow and empirical result is promising. The comments are insightful for us, and we have addressed them in the following response.

- **Q1: Why the prototypical method is effective as the local solver, and what if the representations are single-clustered or the mean prototype is far away from the true mean.**
- **A1:** Thanks for the reviewer’s valuable questions. We note that the prototypical methods have been shown their empirical improvement in centralized noisy-label learning [1-3], so there is empirical foundation to apply the prototypical noise detection. Our finding in this paper is that we find the local prototypical method can be a better local noise detector in FL’s small, imbalanced, and noisy datasets than previous small-loss ones used in FedCorr and RoFL. Note that **we do not directly use GMM on the embeddings**, instead, we first calculate a proxy prototype for each class and then **use GMM in the cosine similarities** between the prototypes and the sample embeddings. We reckon this will be more effective than directly using GMM on the embeddings and we now elaborate the empirical insights about why it works, hoping it could relieve the raised concerns.
- For a given class, there exist two kinds of samples, the clean ones and the noisy ones. The clean samples have similar feature spaces, thus they will have similar embeddings (i.e. representations) and their averaged embedding is strengthened in certain direction, being close to the true prototype. For the noisy samples, they are from other classes with diverse representations, so their averaged embedding is weaker than the clean averaged embedding. Therefore, the clean averaged embedding will dominate in mean prototype. Knowing that the embeddings are high-dimensional (512 in our paper) and resorting to the fact that any two high-dimensional random vectors are most probably orthogonal, the cosine similarities between the noisy embeddings and the mean prototype are likely to be closer to zero, while the clean samples will have higher cosine values, closer to 1. Hence, the cosine similarities tend to have two Gaussians, one smaller for the noisy samples and the larger for the clean. We gave empirical evidence in Figure 1,3,4 of the initial submission and we add additional evidence on the Figure 6-8 Appendix A.2 during the revision.
- Based on the above analysis, we can answer the reviewer’s questions. Firstly, if the noisy representations are single-clustered, the cosine similarities will not be single-clustered, because the clean samples will strengthen each other and the high-dimensional property of embeddings will make the cosine values more distinguishable. Secondly, it is acceptable if the mean representation is far from the true mean, as long as the cosine angles between clean samples and the mean prototype are smaller than the angles of the noisy ones. And this is reasonable since the clean samples have similar directions, that they will dominate in the mean prototype. Therefore, our method is not ad-hoc as the reviewer may concern; instead, it is general and robust in most FL noisy learning settings.
- **Q2: Whether the usage of two-component GMM is unrealistic.**
- **A2:** Thanks for the advice. As we mentioned in the last response, we assumed the cosine similarities have two Gaussians not the embeddings itself. We empirically visualized the similarity distributions in Figure 1, and the GMM is able to effectively recognize two Gaussian with convergence and better performance. In the revision, we display more detailed results in Appendix A.2 to show the effectiveness of GMM. As the reviewer suggested, other non-parametric methods would also be interesting in our scenarios, and we would like to study it in future work.

content.title: Followup to Reviewer ojgr:
content.comment:
Thank you very much for your feedback.

We clarify that implementing GMM on cosine similarities or other scalars is not weird but common and natural.

- FedCorr [1] and DivideMix [2] apply GMM on samples’ loss to distinguish noisy and clean samples.
    - FedCorr further uses GMM on a borrowed LID value to distinguish noisy and clean clients.
    - However, the setting of clean and noisy clients only depends on a fixed percentage parameter.
    - Their noise levels across noisy clients follow a uniform distribution instead of a Gaussian.
- Another work [3] applies a beta mixture model (BMM) fitting on samples’ loss to distinguish noisy and clean samples. They also compare the performance of BMM and GMM.
- In CCVR [4], clients calculate the mean and variance of representations for each class. The server uses the aggregated mean and variance to generate virtual representations by a GMM. Then, the server re-trains the classifier for the global model.
- PANM [5] firstly  computes the cosine similarities of gradients to measure the similarities between clients. GMM is fit on the cosine similarities to distinguish the same-clustered neighbors and the different-clustered outliers.

Hence, we are confident that it is natural and feasible for us to apply GMM on the prototypical similarities to distinguish the noisy samples. 

Hoping our response can relieve your concern.

### Reference

content.title: Response to Reviewer ujZf (1/2):
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments. Since this review is released after the first stage of rebuttal, we are confused that whether the reviewer has checked our new version of paper and the rebuttal to other reviewers. Still, we are happy to give detailed responses as follows, hoping they can relieve the reviewer's concerns.

- **Q1: Why the class prototype is defined in the form of Eq. (5)? Is it proposed in the work, or has it been used in other works?**
- **A1:** Thanks for the reviewer’s questions. The prototype definition in our paper is derived from previous works. We note that the definition of the prototype is widely adopted by researchers since a classic work: prototypical network [1]. The meaning is the average of embeddings of a class-wise feature. It has been used in previous peer-reviewed works, e.g., Eq.(3) in [2] and Eq.(2) in [3]. More works that also use this definition but are not related to federated learning or noisy-label learning are not listed here.
- **Q2: Why the noisy samples represent outliers in the embedding space? If a model has fitted the noisy sample, i.e., performed well on the noisy sample, the embedding may not be the claimed outlier.**
- **A2:** Please see [Response to Reviewer ojgr (1/2) A1](https://openreview.net/forum?id=7zxPlqOT5us&noteId=26jT_a0fSWO) for our response.
- **Q3: The definition of Eq. (9) and Eq. (10) is hard to understand. Why construct pseudo labels in this way.**
- **A3:**  We want to make sure that we are going to explain Eq. (9) and Eq. (10) in the latest version of our paper (revision on 18 Nov 2022). 
    - In Eq. (9), we aim to find a class for a noisy sample where the class prototype is the closest to this sample. We compare the cosine distances between this sample and all prototypes in Eq. (9). 
    - In Eq. (10), we first compute the confidence of the pseudo label by a softmax result of cosine distances between this sample and all prototypes. Depending on the dynamic threshold obtained in Eq. (8), we can decide whether to assign a pseudo label to this noisy sample. If confidence is larger than the threshold, change the label. Else, stay unchanged. 
    - The reason to construct pseudo labels by such a prototypical classifier is that in the early rounds, the prototypical classifier has higher accuracy than the model’s classifier, while in the late rounds, the prototypical classifier has comparable accuracy with the model’s classifier. To simplify, we do not switch it but choose a stable prototypical classifier. 
    - A threshold for giving pseudo labels is also a well-known thought in noisy-label learning and semi-supervised learning.
- **Q4: Where is the description for selecting a validation set?**
- **A4:** 
    - We kindly remind the reviewer that in the new version of the paper, we add the details of the validation set (i.e., testing set) in Table 5 of the appendix, e.g., CIFAR10: 50,000 training examples and 10,000 testing examples [4]. 
    - We note that in the federated learning community, except for the personalized FL topics, the default setup of the validation is the global generalization performance, which is indicated by the test accuracy of the global model on a global-objective-consistent dataset. 
        - Initially, the data will be divided into a training set and a validation set. The training set will be split for each client to train. The validation set will be used for global model test accuracy (global generalization performance) in each round. 
        - You can refer classic FL works [2][4][5][6], and recent federated noisy learning works[7][8][9] to confirm.
- **Q5: The reported results seem not averaged with five runs, as I cannot find the standard deviation.**
- **A5:** We apologize for not making it clear. We have done five runs, and the current results are averaged with five runs. But due to the space limitation of the tables, we did not include the standard deviation. We would have made a better clarification if the review had come earlier before the revision deadline.
- **Q6: The experimental settings seem casual, I cannot find any references cited for supporting the employed settings.**
- **A6:** 
    - We clarify that our experimental settings are not casual that we tightly follow the settings in previous works. 
    - Additionally, we note that in the FL community, there may exist a consensus on the default experimental settings. 
        - Therefore, it is common to display without specific references, including datasets, data partition, clients, the optimizer, training rounds, local epochs, local batch size, and so on. 
        - You can refer to [4]-[11] and other FL works to confirm. 
    - Thanks for your caution, we will add the references in the final version. If you have further concerns about the setting of noise labels, please check our Response to [Reviewer ojgr (2/2)](https://openreview.net/forum?id=7zxPlqOT5us&noteId=ZKJde8Tqes).

content.title: After reading all the response and the updated paper
content.comment:
After reading all the reviews, the response and the updated paper, I decrease my score to 3. Overall, I think the problem of defending noisy data in FL is interesting and well motivated in the paper.
However, some claims are without experimental or theoretical supports. The improved performance by setting switching round cannot support learning periods are important in FL. There should be more ablation studies to explore. The low accuracy of pseudo labeling cannot well support the claim of that "early phase of FEDAVG does NOT need to cautiously learn from noisy samples and clients". In addition, as other reviewers point out, the mean embeddings may not be clean representations, and it is not clear how they are trustable. 

Besides, the novelty is still limited. The focus of the improvements lies on the small local datasets. However, cannot the other techniques be applied in small local datasets? And the FL actually hopes to learn a global model from many local datasets. Therefore, the total dataset size is large. Furthermore, as the authors point out in the response, the FL has difficulty in convergence, which is a well-known bottleneck of FL. The proposed techniques that mainly focus on processing local datasets may lose a global view of all datasets, aggravating the convergence problem of FL.

The tested Non-IIDness (a in {1, 0.7}) is relatively low compared with the classical FL works[1,2] (a=0.1).

[2] Federated Learning on Non-IID Data Silos. Li et al. In ICDE 2022.

content.title: Response to Reviewer WMvh (1/2):
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the detailed feedback. However, we suppose the reviewer may have some misunderstandings on our work, and we will give the clarification below.
- **Q1: The low accuracy of pseudo labeling cannot well support the claim of that "early phase of FEDAVG does NOT need to cautiously learn from noisy samples and clients".**
- **A1:** 
    - The sentence you referred is NOT appeared in our paper. We only claim “we cautiously aggregate clients’ model parameters according to the noise levels.” 
    - In addition, because of the low accuracy of pseudo labeling in the early phase, we adopt pseudo labeling later. It does not mean there is no need for cautiously learning in the early stage; as we state in the paper, in the early stage, we also adopt the Denoise Mixup Loss and the Prototypical Similarity Loss, which are robust in noisy environments; the only difference is that the labels of the detected noisy samples are still the given labels in the early.
- **Q2: The mean embeddings may not be clean representations, and it is not clear how they are trustable.**
- **A2:** 
    - We have provided explanations and specific experiment results of the performance of the prototype and GMM.
    - The experiments also show its effectiveness, especially advantages on baselines, which is significant. 
    - If the reviewer is still confused with the behind mechanism, it is recommended to read our response in [Response to Reviewer ojgr (1/2) A1](https://openreview.net/forum?id=7zxPlqOT5us&noteId=26jT_a0fSWO).
- **Q2: Cannot the other techniques be applied in small local datasets?**
- **A2:** Existing works all fail to fit the small local datasets in FL.
    - Simply borrowing approaches from centralized learning is ineffective, as the experiment results of Co-teaching[1] and DivideMix [2] in our paper. 
    - Existing federated noisy learning works’ small-loss trick [3][4] is also a borrowed method without any modification and reconsideration. As the results we showed, it is not accurate.
    - We consider the unique challenges in FL to present the current method. At this point, our techniques are effective in small local datasets and surpass baselines. It is also open for future works to give more methods working on FL’s small, imbalanced and noisy local datasets.
- **Q3: The proposed techniques that mainly focus on processing local datasets may lose a global view of all datasets, aggravating the convergence problem of FL.**
- **A3:** 
  - Using local methods to solve global problems is an important direction of federated learning research [5][6]. 
    - Especially in FedRoD [6], the authors find that individually solving the local class imbalance problems on each client will result in a more generic (generalized) global model, thus, further improving local personalization. 
    - Similar results are concluded in our paper in FL with noisy labels. 
  - Moreover, we do not _"lose a global view"_, and the reviewer may ignore our contribution in the robust global aggregator in Section 4.3. 
  - Last but not least, our method HAS GREAT improvement in the convergence of the global model. 
    - The reviewer can find our convergence results in Fig. (2) of the main paper. It is quite obvious that our method has the BEST convergence results compared with baselines and it is EVEN COMPARABLE with "FedAvg without noisy samples". 
    - Therefore, we are so confused about how the reviewer jumps to the conclusion that our method is "aggravating the convergence problem of FL".
- **Q4:** **The tested Non-IIDness (a in {1, 0.7}) is relatively low compared with the classical FL works[1,2] (a=0.1).**
- **A4:** Firstly, we want to point out that the paper[7] ([2] in the reviewer's citation) adopts $α$=0.5 instead of $α$=0.1 (mentioned by the reviewer). It seems that the reviewer had a wrong citation. In fact, once an $α$ below 1, it is quite imbalanced, as shown in our Fig. (5). And an $α$ of 10 or 100 looks very balanced.
    - In view of baselines, FedCorr’s [4] experiments are mainly conducted in IID settings with only one small table of Non-IID CIFAR-10, $α$={1,10}; RoFL [3] and RHFL [8] both only adopt IID settings. We conduct all experiments under Non-IID data distribution on both CIFAR10/100, with label noises. We give better results with much lower values $α$ than the baselines. It is a great contribution on the noisy labeling problem in FL community.
    - In view of other FL works, here are some examples of peer-reviewed works:  FedDyn [9] uses $α$={0.6,0.3}, CReFF[10] uses $α$={0.5}, FedFTG[11] uses $α$={0.6, 0.3}, RSCFed[12] uses $α$={0.8}. The $α$=0.1 mentioned by you is acceptable, while other values below 1 are also widely adaptable. We do not agree that ours are relatively low. Other FL works are without our challenges of noisy labels, and our value of $α$ does not make a huge difference with theirs.
    - We are pleased to provide a further observation when $α$=0.1 in the final version.
